Sponsor: Thermal Grizzly Contact Frame - https://geni.us/Yj6WI
The NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4080 16GB video card provides a firm visual definition of the word "disappointing," mostly because its performance does climb from the RTX 3080 in meaningful ways, but the price climbs in lock-step. This leaves the 4080 simply stagnating versus the RTX 3080 while pulling the ladder up further on GPU prices. Older RX 6950 XT and RTX 3080 GPUs at lower prices further sap the value of the RTX 4080 16GB, not to mention the weird misstep of launch-unlaunching the RTX 4080 12GB (a different model).

comments.text: @ZFPS115  I agree, and I dislike upscaling in general, but I have found DLSS to be useful on my laptop (which has a 3060).  Helps get settings closer to what I'm used to on my main gaming PC while preserving framerates.  And if Nintendo were to introduce an upgraded Switch that could do DLSS, that (the handheld area) is one that could benefit.  I definitely agree that upscaling is, for the most part, getting out of hand though, especially on consoles.  We have people reporting consoles as "running at native 4k" when they are ALL upscaling, and it's all fake.  And the reports that DLSS/FSR can look better than native resolution are absolutely ridiculous.  Native resolution ALWAYS looks better than upscaling.  Always.  100% of the time.  I don't care how good your upscaling is.  The best it can possibly ever do is "looks good/close enough".  People saying that whatever upscaling they're using looks better than native are 100% lying.

This issue is coming from the fact that the new series of cards provides such a huge increase in speed over the previous series.  In prior cycles I could easily go 3-4 years between upgrades this was typically 2 series releases.  The new cards never presented THAT much of an increase in speed over the previous version.  For example the jump from 970 to 1070 was not a massive difference.

Now it seems every year there is a new series and an upgrade so large that you feel the need to upgrade and this causes a dilemma for NVidia.  They can no longer price their cards similarly priced as the previous series when there is such a huge increase in speed.  If they priced the 4080 at $800 they would never sell the rest of their 3080.

comments.text:
I compare the "progress" with the video cards to the "progress" in physical movie media.      VHS was improved on tremendously when DVDs came out, the improvement that Blu-rays had on DVDs was noticeable but not as impressive as the move from VHS to DVD.      4K was supposed to replace Blu-rays, but you can watch videos out there where they put the images side by side, and the change is minimal, with situations where the transfer to disk is actually superior for the Blu-ray over the 4K transfer.      Whatever eventually replaces 4K (8K?) will be even less of an incremental improvement.      

I have a 4K TV that I use as a monitor for the limited gaming that I do using a GTX 1080ti card and it handles everything that I throw at it fairly well.     I do periodic comparisons to the new cards that come out and generally there is a 15% or so increase in performance each new generation, but there really isn't a compelling reason for me to upgrade the card (assuming it will even fit in my case) at considerable expense since what I currently have is doing a great job.    For the vast majority of the gamers out there, there isn't a compelling reason to upgrade beyond a card that does a decent job of handling 1080P and/or 4K.     

IMO, both the video card and movie physical media providers are needing something "new" and "special" to justify product improvements.      For the physical media companies, it could be something like an 8K display with glasses free 3D.     IDK what it would take to move the video card demand.       From what I have read, the human eye generally sees in the 5K-15K range, depending on whether we are scanning (eyes moving) or focusing on something (eyes not moving).      That is why I threw in glasses free 3D bundled with an 8K resolution - there isn't enough justification for people to replace their existing and still working 1080P and 4K TVs without something beyond just a resolution improvement.       I got curious about this and took the 4K TV I was using as a monitor and set it up next to my 1080P TV in the living room, both 17' away from the couch where I watched.      I didn't see any difference in the pictures from that distance, although I could when I moved closer.

We can bitch as much as we want and be right about it. But we forget one basic thing.

RTX 4080 is a premium gpu but not the highest end. Still it has 45+ billion transistors. Paired with a 12900k or 13900k , the bill reaches something in excess of 55 probably 60 billion transistors..
Please take into account that even this is not a fair comparison for PCs as Intel processors are still stuck at a node process inferior to  that of nvidia gpus. But let's stick to this example for the sake of clarity.

If a 13900k costs 500 dollars and rtx 4080 say, 600 to 800 dollars , then you can effectively assemble a pc with 1700ish to 2000 ish dollars that outperforms M1 max by a considerable margin.
So, performance conscious consumers would not even look at the "premium" products Apple and Microsoft had to offer . It would be nonsensical and a disruption to their business paradigm. 
Because who would buy a surface or a mac book pro , when you could have multiple times the performance with same money or less? No-one.

That was the situation circa 2000-2010, that is why these "premium" products were a curiosity back then. I bet Satya Nadella and Tim Cook are raging behind closed doors feeling threatened once again. Even at these prices pc components are starting to smoke the until recently "lifestyle" "premium" products.

Also , pc component makers feel like idiots for themselves under this situation. Why offer a much superior product and sell it at a much inferior price.? "Since sheep will buy premium apple and microsoft solutions let them buy ours as well, at a much higher cost."

comments.text:
Nvidia has almost no incentive whatsoever to sell these cards for a penny less than they’re currently selling for. That’s because there are enough people out there who are willing to pay whatever Nvidia decides to charge. 

If Nvidia is making as many cards as they can and there are lines in front of every store and the cards sell out within hours, why on earth would Nvidia even consider reducing their prices? 

I agree that the prices are getting crazy but economically, the cards are “worth” whatever people are willing to pay for them. 

Nvidia saw tons of people paying double or even triple the retail prices of 3000 series cards for the last two years and they watched a bunch of scalpers make tons of money selling on eBay. Of course they were going to jack the prices of 4000 series cards up. They just had two years of seeing people pay 2-3 times the retail prices and adjusted the retail prices for the next gen cards accordingly. 

The 4000 series cards are selling out almost immediately, even at these higher prices. If they had priced the 4090 at $799, they’d sell out just as quickly but Nvidia would only make half the money. 

The only thing that’s going to force Nvidia to bring their prices back down to earth is legitimate competition from AMD and the willingness of consumers to buy Radeon instead of GeForce. Nvidia is going to have to lose a meaningful portion of their market share in order for them to even consider bringing their prices back down. And even if people started buying AMD cards in massive numbers, I could still easily see Nvidia keeping their flagship model prices 40-50% higher than AMD’s flagship prices just because for the high end cards, Nvidia will likely always have enough people who are willing to pay whatever price they want to charge.

comments.text:
A tangent here, but the ridiculous framerates you can reach with "Siege" (not Rainbow Six) kinda makes me sad, as someone who was forcing "Rainbow Six: Vegas", a Core2-optimized game, to run on a struggling Pentium 4. - I mean, it just shows how much it's not a game for its (sort of) cutting-edge graphics and "adventure" anymore, but leaning much more into optimization for being e-sports compatible. - Impressive, sure, but the Tom Clancy type games should be tactical campaign-games that also have eye-candy. - Save from the first few games, these used to be Unreal Engine games, you know. And while I think Ubisoft's proprietary engines are quite cool (and I actually commend studios for doing that over going the "generic" route of Unreal or Unity) it just feels forced for this one and they also watered down what Anvil can even do. I mean, that's the "Assassin's Creed" engine, which, no matter what you think of the games, can do some amazing awe-inspiring stuff.
But "Siege" has been so "simplified" that it looks more like a higher-end Source Engine game or something. - I'd be the first to admit that the "Vegas" ones have some really ugly things in them, mostly the textures (though, that was probably more due to the games becoming more console-focused and PC-versions didn't get any "upgrades") and some of the angular models (but that's like 2005/2006 for ya). STILL, they had some spectacle and flair to them, especially in the more "commercial" areas like the Vegas Strip and inside of casinos and the like. - Back then, I was really thinking like "Man, think of what a Rainbow Six could look like in a few years.", but then the next thing was "Siege" all the way in 2015. - Thanks, Ubisoft. - Oh well... Rant over.

comments.text:
While price to performance ratio is important, but I also feel like efficiency should also be just as important, especially as efficiency will contribute to cost of ownership over time. Sure, these cards may be slightly more efficient than the 3080, but are they more efficient enough to be justifiable. It's a triangle of price, performance, and power where the companies should be aiming for a scope within the center of the triangle, not a scope within a vertex or edge of the triangle, and having generational reductions in price and power while having performance uplift  that fit the same scope. Say, for example, a generational change makes a GPU cheaper but it's highly inefficient, over the lifetime of the card the worse efficiency will result in higher bills, not just electrical but also cooling within the relevant months of the year, that may contribute to a higher overall price by time you buy a new GPU. And yes, I know cost of living varies and isn't entirely consistent year to year, but it's still an important aspect when determining value of a product that directly contributes to bills. I also think it'd be important to look at efficiency over the full sweep of performance, from idle to full tilt, from properly cooled to thermal throttled, etc., as benchmarking is just one data point across this spectrum, and realistic use of components will cover the full spectrum of use cases, which then also ties back into why efficiency and long term costs are important aspects when considering value; say, for a hypothetical, a GPU is less efficient under lower loads than it is comparatively at higher loads, this may not seem like an important point until you consider that not every game is super demanding, that the owner won't be gaming 24/7 and the GPU may be relegated to hardware acceleration for other tasks such as a browser, it's these realistic use points that end up mattering more over time when efficiency is concerned, and again that feeds into long term costs of ownership. 

I want to see the consumer side of this industry to actually care about the full picture, not just upfront costs of upgrading. This argument is also supported by the existence of efficiency cores in CPUs. Price to performance is an important topic, but so is power to performance, and price to power, again it's a triangle that would optimally have a balanced scope.

"One percent more performance if you spend one percent more money makes it not interesting" (I'm paraphrasing) is wrong I think. It's like saying that card should be evaluated based on $/frame when it's $/(frame-60) that should matter. 

A 500$ card that does 60 fps at medium graphics on 2022 AAA games will last 1 year if your minimum standard is medium graphics and 60 fps. A 1200$ card that does 120 fps at medium graphics on 2022 AAA games will last at least 3 years before not being capable of keeping with that minimum standard. 

So, 2.4 times the price but will last at least 3 times longer. Which would make that hypothetical 1200$ card the better deal.

I may very well be wrong tho.

comments.text:
I think there is a bigger issue here, which is "at what point do we currently need so much more performance?".   Previous gen GPU products (3080,3090, 6900, etc) and current gen CPU products are essentially more than most common users will need for the foreseeable future.   Meaningful 8k gaming is pretty far away still, and VR is also still an expensive fantasy for most of us.   There  is very little driving consumers to these new GPUs except perhaps the need to take a few virtual inches onto an otherwise tiny apprentice.   The games are for the most part not there, Unity and other gaming engines aren't really there yet, and developers using those platforms will be a year or two behind that.  So what we have here is actually a product with no natural demand outside of perhaps people doing heavy video renders or 3D work.  

This may be the Windows 8.1 moment for GPUs, the improvement nobody needed.

So like everything it all depends on what you are doing.  A great example of a game and mode where there is literally no such thing as too much GPU right now is DCS in high end VR. Granted ED needs to get off their butts and optimize as well as add in multi core and Vulkan but as it stands today you get a noticeable jump even going from a 3090 to a 4090 in that use case.  Obviously that isn't for everyone and yes there are many games where the 3080-3090 cards are plenty fine thus 40 series would just be pure overkill.

Especially at this stupid price for a 4080.  Obviously they left much room for a Ti but without adjusting pricing they would be making a product that wouldn't compete against a 4090 yet it's pricing would be so close to a 4090 that there would be no good reason to buy a Ti over a 4090. Either way Steve's advise here is solid.  Just hold on to your money and wait for RDNA3 to drop and perhaps down the road for a 4080 Ti to see how the pricing ends up.  The 4080 at 1200 is just stupid money for the performance.

1) How much stutter the AMD cards produce at 7:11 in a very popular MMO, FF14, at 4k compared to NVidia cards. Look at those horrible .1% lows - 36% worse, below 30FPS!
2) Ditto for TW: WH 3 at 4k. 25% spread in .1% lows!
3) Stuttery performance again in Control at 1440p where the game is playable at 60+FPS on the 3080 but has crazy stuttering on the 6950XT. 3080 has 38% better .1% dips and stays above 60 while the 6950XT grinds down to 46 FPS once every 15 seconds on average. This is probably manifested by an irritating stutter/hiccup a few times a minute.
4) The games where the 6950XT was neck-and-neck with the 3080 were console ports -- ones where I've never once met anyone who has played them. Certainly not a good representation of total PC gaming time globally.
5) MSRP dollar per frame is on a curve and NVidia has set that curve, AMD is still below it for the 10th year running. Now that Eth mining is kaput, MSRP will be relevant again for pricing and NVidia will not only still be the most stable and best in professional work, it will be the best per dollar again in actual games people are playing.

The fact that NVidia is pricing the increased performance up as if it's all one generation of tech, like you mentioned at the end with your needle analogy, is because AMD CAN'T compete. I want AMD to compete so NVidia gets its prices back down below $1000 for their xx80 cards, but the fact of the matter is that AMD doesn't compete and its for reasons you can get a glimpse of in this video. It would behoove AMD to improve its GPUs and drivers instead of pushing developers of niche games they perform competitively on to bake in a benchmark test so that review outlets grab enough AMD-favored benchmarks to trick a small amount of buyers into buying AMD.

comments.text:
No dude that 15% inflation since the launch of Ampere is laughable.  That's an inflation figure that's used basically to establish cost of living raises for people getting govt. benefits like pensions and Social Security, but that's not a REAL inflation rate.

That number goes off the theory that if beef is too expensive, you buy chicken, or to better say it if steak is too expensive, you buy ground beef.  And what I'm saying is factual.  This is REALLY what the govt. does.  It means over time a person who lives on SS loses the ability to survive on their pensions/SS.

I can look at food prices across the board and know that I'm paying about 30 - 50% more in general for a typical product, with some being less and some products being almost double of what they used to cost.

And the same is true with general merchandise.  25% is about a minimal figure for REAL inflation.  Now, the reason this hasn't hit CPUs in particular is because both AMD and Intel had higher profit margins and they've had to reduce profit margins.  But there's a second factor to CPUs vs. other electronics that have large PCBs and lots of electronic components on them.  A CPU is very small.  So, while TSMC or Intel has higher costs per wafer, you get a lot more die out of each wafer going from something like TSMC N7 to N5.  This helps to compensate for higher wafer costs since I get more die from the wafer.  And for a CPU, this is a BIG part of the cost, the actual die.  For a GPU on the other hands, NOW you have inflation of MANY products, the cost for all the electronic components, the cost of the PCB, the cost of making that BIG hunk of an air cooler, the fan shroud.

So, both AMD and Nvidia are experiencing about a REAL inflation rate for making products of about 25%.  AMD is offsetting this a little by moving to MCM and using a less expensive node for cache and I/O.  This also help with failure rate since all the die is much smaller.  On the other hand Nvidia has a HUGE die, and it's on the most expensive node Nvidia has.

I'm not trying to justify Nvidia's behavior.  I don't really like the company because I think they're about the most greedy of Nvidia, Intel and AMD and certainly have the highest profit margin.  But their REAL inflation rate is probably closer to 25%.  So, the launch price of a 4080 should be around $875 based on inflation over the 3080.  And for those who are going to talk about features, I'd say that's typical, and because they went from Samsung 8N to TSMC N4 they gain a MASSIVE uplift for transistor density.  So, this is a typical part of a generational uplift.

comments.text:
@lifemocker85  Dude you keep misunderstanding. I'm talking about games that are intrinsically locked to 60. There are a ton of console ports like this, also low-demand indie games, etc. People with flagship cards don't restrict themselves to playing only massive AAA gpu-suckers, they play whatever seems fun. Having the card means you can play those games when you want to, not that you have to.

Also, a card like a 3090 can play an awful lot of games at hundreds of FPS, sometimes a thousand or more in an older or less-demanding game if your CPU doesn't suck. Unless your monitor is capable of playing at, say, 522fps, your system is still gonna end up capping your framerate at some number, be it 120, 144, 240, whatever. Even with variable refresh rate there's still a maximum.

And finally, modern Windows versions all use the GPU for desktop composition, browsers usually do GPU acceleration by default, not to mention stuff like video decoding, which is needed a lot of the time when browsing the web. That means you're actively using your GPU to various extents nearly all the time, rather than letting it idle in a power-saving state near sleep. Obviously it's probably being utilized at a very low rate, but the tech can't run the clock all the way down to 1MHz, so there IS a minimum amount of processing going on,  and it's going to be fewer watts to run that clock rate on a newer card.

Edit: Just found some documentation that suggests a 3090 idles (meaning when it's not being used AT ALL, not even for the use cases in the previous paragraph) at 30W, while the 4090 idles at 25W. I'm not sure how well that difference scales up when it's more active, but that would definitely suggest that, over several years of ownership, you're going to pay maybe a hundred bucks less for realistic day-to-day boring usage and maybe a few hundred less to power the GPU while playing the kinds of games I'm talking about.

Power costs are not insignificant, and if you're tight on money, they're something you really want to think twice about, because they'll bite you on the butt if you're not careful about your power draw.

Get yourself one of those Kill-a-Watt style inline plug+monitor things and look up your local power rates, you'll see what I mean.

comments.text:
My GPU purchases over the last 16 years.

2006 XFX 7900 GTX 512MB @ £89.99 X 2 in SLI
2008 LEADTEK GTX260 896MB @ £146.99
2012 EVGA GTX660Ti 2GB @ £225.00
2014 ASUS STRIX GTX980 OC 4GB @ £350.00

That's where it ends, and frankly I need another Maxwell moment to happen because I've wanted to upgrade for 3 or 4 years now, but I look at what I'd get for the money and just shake my head. I have plenty of money to spend, but I absolutely hate myself when I spend that money on something and don't feel like it was a good deal. 

I'd have to really need to spend that money to hand it over, and I'm so glad to have accumulated hundreds of games in the last 20 years that I still enjoy playing. I managed to play through RDR2 1080p locked 30fps and it was absolutely fine, but the clock is ticking and there will come a game that forces my hand at some point.

I had an Alienware Area 51m laptop in 2003, and Area51 desktop in 2005 prior to building my own, so I've been a PC gamer for 20 odd years now.

I actually bought my sisters unused PS4 slim and VR last Xmas for £100 and spent this year playing all the exclusive games I'd missed out on over the years, and it has been awesome, so much so that I just can't see me splashing out twice the cost of a console just to get a GPU nowadays, it's frustrating to say the least, but that's where we are.

Here's hoping for more sensible times ahead, I look forward to the day Steve makes a video sounding the all clear.

@charlesbrunelle2831  $500 card would be more than enough for most people for several years. That is faster than a PS5, so I wouldn't call it antiquated in a year. You can't place any particular price bracket or performance level as a minimum standard. People play a variety of games, at various settings and resolutions, and gameplay styles. What would be completely unacceptable for some might be extreme overkill for many others. With the quality of graphics from modern games, even medium settings are fine for many. New games may have the same graphical quality at what is considered lower settings, so just because a card from today doing high in many games can do only medium 3 years later, doesn't mean the card produces low quality graphics all of a sudden, but games crank up polygons and effects for those who have high end cards.

Not everyone demands to play every game at 4K ultra 200 FPS, and is willing and able to spend $1000 every year to do so. Technology has evolved to where "midrange" cards produce very good visuals. Similar to cell phones, they are fast enough now that 99% of people would realistically be fine with most $3-500 phones, and $1000 plus phones are a complete waste. So having a chart showing average FPS/$ would be ideal, doing otherwise skews the data and introduces bias.

comments.text:
The past couple years proved that people will buy out whatever's put in front of them, especially from Nvidia.  It's  kind of hard to fault them for at least testing the waters on how far they can go.  I don't think even they knew that there were so many willing buyers out there.  A halo product like the 3090 that was traditionally only supposed to be tech showcase and for production type workloads?  Tom's Hardware, August 04, 2021: "Nvidia's RTX 3090 Has Apparently Sold More Units Than AMD's Entire RX 6000 Series Lineup."  A global pandemic that you would expect to drive people's spending down across the board?  Instead, people spending multiple times MSRP to instantly buy out any GPU Nvidia put into the market.  Yeah, they made a massive miscalculation on a sizable chunk of their market, cryptominers, and that's left them with excess 30-series inventory they need to clear.  So, they're pricing 40-series to take care of that extra inventory.  It makes sense.  But, really, when you look at the big picture, they were massively underpricing the 3080 and 3070 for no real reason.  They didn't know it.  We didn't know it.  But now we do.  They kind of stumbled on to the right price for a product with the 3090 at $1500, something that everyone would have thought was silly at the time.

It's not that I like it.  Not at all.  But, man, you really can't argue the numbers.  30-series sold like hotcakes in the worst possible world situation.  AMD doesn't have the mindshare in the GPU market.  Intel's beyond a joke.  Nvidia's marketing has thoroughly succeeded at gassing up ray-tracing even though it's still irrelevant to almost everyone.  And on top of that, literally everyone's using TSMC to fab everything anyway, so there's not a whole lot that can be done to change the supply side of the equation.  Steve and crew are exactly right to point out the disappointing nature of the beast here and put objective numbers to it.  But supply and demand ultimately set price, and they've set a high one.

comments.text:
I think I have commented this before under some other video, but I switched from nVidia to AMD in january of 2021. I had a long story with nVidia, from MX440 to 7600GS-8800GTS-9800GT-GTX260-480-2x GTX Titan SLI-GTX1080-RTX2080Ti. But now I run a 6900XT and is very likely to get a 7900XTX, and not a 4080. Because I am disappointed. I always had a moderate bias towards "team green" products, but things change and sometimes not for the better. nVidia seems to have embraced that "not for the better" led by their insatiable greed fuelled by superior raytracing capabilities.

It is most unfortunate that AMD chose to, at large, ignore raytracing improvements in their new architecture - the boost in their presentation was in line with rasterization performance boost: 1.5-1.7x compared to 69(5)0. This is not enough for competitive challenge to 4090 and most likely even 4080 in RT. And RT is the stuff these days. Because in rasterization even modern top of the line cards can do satisfactorily, and raytracing is where that extra "umph" is needed the most. Unfortunately, with how AMD 7000 GPU series turned out to be (according to their presentation), we will not see big RT boosts, and that gives nV headroom to put ridiculous prices on their x80 and x90 series, because even though 7900 might beat 4080 in raster, in raytracing they are unrivaled, and the gamer with the buck would almost always choose a full-feature product rather than one that is better in one aspect but lacks in another.

@Demon09-_-  For as much shit as it got on launch, it was the best (or second best depending on where the 6600 was priced) performance per dollar (raw gaming performance) GPU in the new market for quite a while.  Even in a pcie 3.0 system, it's still faster than a base 1650 and on a 4.0 rig, it roughly matches the 1650 Super.  I had the misfortune of a shorted gfx + mobo at the start of the year (a cat barfing over top of a high airflow case == bad, smelly things), so right at the height of GPUs being crazy expensive.  1650 Supers were hitting $400 USD (sometimes more) and 3050's were hitting $500, so I got a sata SSD, a used optiplex, and a 6500xt with the plan of upgrading the machine to a 12100f (which I've done since).  In the optiplex I was able to play everything I wanted, even cyberpunk and RDR2, though cyberpunk was throttled on the CPU side in certain scenes.  Speaking from experience, yes, it performs better in pcie 4.0 (which new budget builds should support, especially if you're going to pair it w/ a 6500xt or 6400), but it's certainly not unplayable in an older machine if someone needs a card on a strict budget at $160.

My point though was that nvidia doesn't want to serve the budget market at all, and they've been actively working to kill it  There was no 2050, no 2030, or even a 1630 until very recently.  The 3050 is a die harvested 3060 that was never meant to actually hit it's MSRP (hell, even now it's $290 new).  What were the last budget releases from nvidia?  The abysmal 1630 a couple of months ago that's way overpriced (It's about $20 shy of the 6500xt and the 6400 walks all over the 1630), or the 3050 that's never seen anything more than token availability at MSRP (a few units of direct to consumer EVGA cards was about it), let alone hit a sub $200 budget bracket, and likely never will.

comments.text:
@M340B58  I kinda feel like defending you, you seem fairly reasonable and not just the classic brainless consumer with more money than sense, even though I wouldn't agree with all your actions. I see your point that having the option is nice, but it's risky as well, as this could theoretically lead to the stagnation in price-performance, just continuing to offer higher "tiers" and needing to spend more to get higher performance.* "TheGamefaq" already mentioned that.

Would I buy an RTX 4090 over a 4080 with plenty of money at hand and a use-case for the performance? Yes. Would I buy it over a 3090? Ofc. Would I buy a 3090 over a 3080, at least the 12 GiB variant (for gaming)? No. Would I buy a ~$4k GPU with twice the performance of a 4090 over it? No.
Why? Linear increases are okay if you have the money to spend**, but I would not spend a huge premium over small increments (3090/3080 = 10% for +100%) and I would also not want to support prices getting out of hand for the given product category ($4K for just a GPU [for gaming]??), even if performance increases reasonably as well.

The market prices out the typical mid-range gamer, the $200-250 GPU market is almost dead and it seemed to be the primary market about 10 years ago (don't know the statistics though). Normal inflation (2% target) would have shifted this range to $250-300, not to probably $500 with the coming gen or already close to $400. And I don't think salary/buying power has increased proportionally, although again I didn't check statistics (probably should soon).

Our spending habits have an effect on the market, so perhaps one should think twice about not so reasonable purchases

Also, I don't really get why you'd need a 4090 for UWQHD. Although I'm not informed about 21:9 resolutions, I'd think a 3080 does plenty fine there, reaching about 100fps in SP AAA titles and an excess of frames in MP titles where it matters more. Is that not the case?

* This might not be viable in practice, if the market is not going with it and there is almost no demand. Also, if the common GPU power stops increasing, software developers need to adapt. Actually this might have upsides, but let's not go into that.. :D
** Not meaning that you can barely afford it and probably shouldn't spend the money for that. I have the feeling there are quite some people buying top-end hardware for the ego and not really being good with money.

This is what I don't get. Let's just pretend for a moment that the 3080 was actually a 3080 Ti, so the "3080 for $1,119". Would the value be better?

Sure, the performance per dollar is the same between the 3080 and 4080. But you could also look at it as: the 3080 was a outlier, no? Same with the 1080 Ti at the time. People drew all sorts of comparisons between the 2080 Super and 1080 Ti, for only being 10% more performance for the same price. 

I'm not trying to defend Nvidia here, but I'm also trying to push for: We should have a standard calculation for price/performance and determine value per-generation. Just like how you'd calculate acceleration based on velocity, can we not do the same for price/performance, and see the "acceleration" of value and how it deviates over time?

Like really, at the end of the day, the SKU numbers don't matter. What matter is the actual price/performance numbers. So how come so many people are talking about it but not actually providing a graph showing performance per dollar based on MSRP. Or even better, an extra graph that shows the current average market price for new, as well as used? If we are worried about value, why not actually spend the time to do market data gathering to show people the current best value?

comments.text: Why not include VR titles in these reviews?  I totally agree with the "stagnation" comments when applied to 2D games when you're just going from 150FPS to 200FPS (or even 60FPS to 100FPS).  Is it really worth it to pay $1200 for a new card when your already at "good enough" framerates.  But in VR going from 60FPS to 90FPS (or even 30FPS to 60FPS in MSFS) can be absolutely worth paying $1200 since it makes an easily visible, practical, and even playable vs. unplayable difference.  In fact, there's almost no reason for me to upgrade from my 2080Ti to a 4080 or 4090 for any of the 2D games I typically play because the value proposition just isn't there; however, in VR, the value proposition is judged entirely differently since 90 fps is a critical comfort threshold in VR, and being able to play certain titles at 120 fps would be amazing.  So, please, please, please, include VR in future reviews.  I realize most people play 2D games, but I suspect that some of the people who benefit the most from these expensive cards (and have the budgets to afford them), are high-end VR enthusiasts like me and would be interested is seeing at least a couple VR benchmarks thrown in here.

comments.text:
"Future Proofing" can have many meanings. Most folks appear to mean "buying big now, when I can, so that I won't have to later" which is a dubious assertion but can at least make sense in the moment (probably wrong but at least it can make sense).

The other way to "future proof" is just to go back in time and buy the products that actually stood the test of time. Since we can't actually time travel this just means looking at the currently available products that were high end a few years ago that are still doing great but cost a ton less than bleeding edge products. If those older products really were "future proof" sort of products then we are currently in those products' future and the time to buy them would be now, if you need a new one, and get three or four years good years out of them for substantially less money than when they were new.

Thanks to garbage market conditions, growing money troubles in our communities, and nothing compelling beyond performance that changes very little on my end and does so for truly insulting price demands (I can afford it but I ain't paying for it) I think my best "future proofing" strategy is to just go into the past.

If one was future proofing with a 3080 or 6950 a year ago then one could, probably, just easily ride that cheaper future proof coat tail for years to come. That there is something "better" out there is irrelevant if what you have does what you need and want.

If I were making money on these cards I would, of course, just figure out the best card that covers the greatest need and pass the cost on as best I could (if I could). My needs are currently covered by my 3060 12GB, that I got for the low, low, price of "free", and absolutely nothing here is compelling to me at all. Given the power of the 3060 and the cost I paid for it this mean that, effectively, it mud stomps even the 4090 as the 4090 can, quite literally, give me nothing I am lacking but do it in a way that I am maximally spending a fortune for that nothing. 

I already refuse to spend $1600 on even the 4090's performance. I could spend it, can afford it, but absolutely will never buy that card for that kind of cost. 

The truth is though, to get the kind of numbers seen in these charts, on the kind of hardware I currently have, I will have to upgrade most of that hardware, too. Which means, for me, I must add taxes, actual cost (many here report much higher than MSRP pricing esp. in Australia and Europe), delivery (if ordered online without shipping covered), along with new board, memory, cpu (and possibly new power supply depending on what the GPU requires) ... all to get a top end that is so ridiculously powerful that I'd also need a new monitor just to get even half of any of that performance realized in any real way. All of which means that these cards just add up to one giant "nope" for me.

From what I can tell there is a massive market out there for a kind of product that neither Nvidia nor AMD seem to be making or even trying to make. If I were Intel I would ignore, for now, the silly top end and focus on that sweet $200-$800 market that wants less of all of this and more of what isn't being focused on at all.

I will say, though, that if the last 3 years have shown us anything it is that MSRP doesn't mean anything anymore so we should stop paying any attention to it. @Gamers Nexus : how about just using "representative pricing AND availability at the time of recording" to compare new product values. We already know that the 4090 will come out on top of all current performance charts ... who cares about that? That isn't news. Let's just cut the aprons on silly MSRP marketing numbers that have no real world meaning and also put some indications on the charts where a "value" shopper might be happy, where a gamer might be happy, and where a professional might be happy? 

The whales and enthusiasts already know where they are as I doubt they ever look much farther than line 3 or 4 on the chart other than too see what cards theirs stomps or what the heck just stomped their current card requiring it to be replaced. The professionals that require CUDA to get their job done also don't care as the top end is just a business expense. 

But all of the rest of us have to dig around a bit through a crap ton of numbers to try to figure out what we might be happy with for products that we are clueless about (which is why we're watching in the first place). And because we don't know we can easily find ourselves lacking the confidence in buying the product best for us because we don't test dozens and dozen of GPUs every year to know any better. I can't figure out what 28% better means to me because I can't tell where on your charts "good enough for me" is.

I know my needs are impossible for you to know but maybe relying on Steam numbers (or something similar) to baseline what folks are actually running might give all of us something to compare to so we can then figure out if "28% faster" is anything, at all, that we are okay with spending hundreds more dollars for.

comments.text:
I'm looking for some advice.

I have an i7 6700k & 1080ti.

Any suggestions on getting a new powerful cpu that'll compliment a gpu upgrade? I plan on getting a 3080.
comments.author: @V_ii

comments.text:
Do you plan on doing any video editing? Or just gaming and surfing the web? What’s your budget? How much do you care about upgrading your CPU while keeping the same motherboard in ~2-3 years?

The new Intel 13600K is probably the best all around CPU available for someone planning on building a new PC from scratch. But it’s been released on a motherboard family that won’t get any newer CPUs moving forward. AMD has pledged to release CPUs that use their new socket for 4-5 years into the future, so theoretically a motherboard you buy today would be usable down the road.

Something also worth noting is price. The newest CPUs benefit from using DDR5 memory instead of DDR4, but this new memory spec is quite expensive at the moment. DDR5 prices are definitely going to come down over the next ~year or so, so it might be worth waiting for the market to settle a bit. This is also applicable to AMD’s newest motherboards, which are surprisingly expensive.

comments.text:
RTX3060: 276mm, $329 at launch
RTX3070: 392mm, $499 at launch
RTX3080: 628mm, $699 at launch
RTX4080: 379mm, $1,199 at launch

The real comparison point should be the RTX3070 here based on die size and cost of manufacturing. The 4080 is WAY cheaper to produce than the 3080 because it is essentially a 70-class die that’s used to make the card. NVidia is getting way more dies per wafer on the 4080 than they are out of the 3080, and even more than the 3070. On a price per square mills meter of GPU die, nVidia has increased pricing > 150% in two years. I’ll give them a pass for the first 15% due to ‘inflation’, but the other 135% is just price gouging, plain and simple.

The lesson here: if you like being ripped off, buy the 4080 and give it a good review (like LTT did).

If you don’t like getting ripped off, give nVidia the Linus Torvalds treatment.

comments.text: You can't really compare CPUs to GPUs. CPUs are much more complex logic oriented, so there's a lot of tricks and optimizations you can do to improve the architecture. GPUs do very "dumb" processing, so it's much harder to get architectural gains, while they've had a ridiculous amount of processing cores for over a decade now, so that's not something they could make use to counter act the death of Moore's law like CPUs could.

@simplyscholar21  i can tell you about the AMD 6800XT experience i have had so far. Got it at release for 750usd. The drivers aren't really a problem unless you get unlucky when windows get a new update. I am someone who reinstall windows every 4-6 months to get the new pc feel. If you do a quick reboot of your windows, there is a chance that some residue from previous drivers are still on the disc to later harass the new install. Use the DDU will most likely fix the issue. This is basically the only scenario when I have had issues with drivers and that one time windows messed things up. That's my driver experience.

You MIGHT experience issues on some old games using direct X11 or older. There is something called DXVK. It forces your game to be translated to Vulkan instead of direct X. You just paste the files into the root folder of the games. This helps performance in older titles.

I have not experienced any performance issues with games from 2013 and newer.

Oh and wanna mod Skyrim? ENBs do hit your fps on AMD cards way more than Nvidia sadly

There are rumours saying that the 7000 series will have better performance in older titles. The performance issue have only been on some games, not all.

So what do I personally think? Price to performance is great. It have its rough edges which can't be ignored on the 6000 cards. Most are fixable but maybe for the average person. It is too much work.

Nvidia will generally give you a more flawless experience in both older and new titles from what I remember from my 1080ti days. Driver issues can happen and it does, people just don't talk about it. You fix them with DDU aswell.
